title: Similarity judge · top-level anchors: where prompt v1 scores well and where it does not

blocks.text:
These views show the judge's top-level anchors, one colour per anchor, with my assessment on each match and a verdict at the top of each block. Click a top-level match (▸) to see the judge's own anchors one level inside it; lines the judge never accounted for are listed above that view.

**Where the prompt works**
- Finding top-level components by responsibility and named code. On Ghostty all eight anchors are correct and 1:1. On Mapping the three runs agree on five of six components.
- Merges scored as grouped (Sol run 2): one anchor against the union of nodes, with the cost kept inside.

**Where it does not**
1. *Grouped vs relocated overlap.* The same merge is scored as grouped (0.862) or as two relocations that double-count v4 lines (0.757).
2. *Partial anchors.* Anchoring a top-level node to part of a branch pushes the leftovers to the top level as unmatched (0.739).
3. *Small sibling sets.* One extra leaf per side halves a two-pair level (Ghostty teardown, 0.48 inside an almost identical subtree).
4. *Ownership changes are free.* History moving under the controller costs ~0.02 when grouped. The verdict text is the only place it shows up.

spec.title: Ghostty S1 ↔ S2 · Astra run 1 · 0.928
spec.explanation:
Verdict: judge is right. All eight top-level anchors are correct and no node is left out. 0.93 is a fair score for two runs of the same prompt. The low teardown score is a formula artefact, but it moves the total by only ~0.02.

Two samples of the same prompt. The judge finds all eight top-level components on both sides, one to one, in the same order, with nothing unmatched. This is the case the rubric is built for and the top-level result is right. The cost sits in two inner levels, and one of those is the formula over-reacting to a small sibling set.

children.comment: The weakness here is in the formula, not the anchoring. This level has two pairs, so one unmatched leaf on each side doubles the denominator from 2 to 4. Two one-line differences cost as much here as a missing component costs at the top. Small sibling sets make Jaccard jumpy, and nothing in the rubric weights by subtree size. Judge's level J = 0.484 = Σs / (pairs + unmatched) = 1.94 / 4.

spec.title: Mapping v2 ↔ v4·2 · Sol run 2 · 0.862 (grouped)
spec.explanation:
Verdict: judge is right. Grouping is the right reading of a merge, and it is the only one of the three runs that accounts for every line of both trees at the top level. One caveat: the ownership change for history (top level in v2, under the controller in v4) costs nothing here (inner 0.96), so the score does not reflect it.

v2 gives CanvasSession and CanvasHistoryService their own top-level nodes. v4 folds CanvasSession into CanvasWorkspace and nests CanvasHistoryService under MappingDocumentController. This run reads both as grouped: one v4 node against two v2 nodes, counted once, with the cost only inside. This is the reading the rubric intends, and the scores of the other runs should be measured against it.

spec.title: Mapping v2 ↔ v4·2 · Sol run 1 · 0.757 (relocated)
spec.explanation:
Verdict: judge is wrong. The anchors are individually plausible, but together they count v4 lines 9–12 and 40–49 twice and penalize a merge as two relocations. Score drops from 0.862 to 0.757, which is about 0.1 for the same structure. The cause is the overlapping grouped/relocated definitions in the prompt.

Same judge, same trees. This time CanvasSession and CanvasHistoryService are anchored separately, to the v4 lines that sit inside other anchors, and marked relocated. The literal rule permits this ("the counterpart exists, but under a different top-level anchor"). The effect is that the v4 lines are counted twice, k goes from 6 to 8, and each extra pair is halved.

spec.title: Mapping v2 ↔ v4·2 · Astra run 2 · 0.739 (partial anchor)
spec.explanation:
Verdict: judge is wrong. Same structure as Sol run 2, but 0.12 lower. A top-level node was anchored to part of a branch, and one leftover child became a top-level unmatched item (+1 in the denominator, s = 0). The prompt says ranges cover the whole subtree, but it also allows anchoring one level deeper, and never says what happens to the rest of the branch.

Groups the workspace and controller the same way as Sol run 2, so the first three anchors agree. The difference is the editor: the judge anchors v2’s top-level MappingEditorRuntime to one child of v4’s presentation branch (B 54–59), then lists one other child (B 66–67) as unmatched at the top level. The rest of that branch (B 53, 60–65, 68–69) is not accounted for anywhere.
